Multivitamins, nutrition, and antiret- roviral therapy for HIV disease in Africa. N Engl J Med 2004; 351: 78–80. INFECTION. Vitamin A has an important role in the prevention of complications from measles (see p.1974), but evidence for benefit in respiratory-tract infections is less compelling (see p.1974). Some studies show evidence of benefit for vitamin C in treating the common cold (p.850), but routine high-dose prophylaxis is not considered justified. Vitamin E has shown conflicting results in respiratory-tract infections, see p.1994. For a discussion of the role of vitamins in HIV infection and AIDS see above. MENTAL FUNCTION. Giving vitamin and mineral supplements to children was reported in 1988 to increase non-verbal intelligence1 and the topic has since remained highly contro- versial. In the next 2 years more studies were published but these failed to substantiate the earlier possible effect and con- cluded that vitamin supplementation did not improve mental functioning or reasoning in children.2,3 Suggestions were made shortly after these publications that there might be a subset of children with poor nutritional status who would re- ceive some benefit4 but this again was disputed.5 In 1991 another study was published,6 this time coinciding with the launch of the proprietary product used in the study, with the publication of a book on the subject, and with the showing on British television of a documentary concerning the study. This study purported to demonstrate that supplementation with exact- ly the recommended dietary allowances of vitamins improved the IQ of children, a finding that was said not to occur signifi- cantly with other quantities of vitamin supplementation. This view attracted extremely harsh criticism7-9 from physicians, nu- tritionists, psychologists, and epidemiologists. Despite conflicting data on the effect of vitamin E intake on cog- nitive decline, US guidelines have suggested that vitamin E be considered in patients with Alzheimer’s disease in an attempt to slow progression of the disease. A subsequent large trial found no benefit for vitamin E over placebo (see Dementia, p.1994). A cohort study found low folate concentrations to be the predomi- nant risk
